name: diagram-generator
description: House style for Mermaid diagrams used across course notes — automata/Turing-machine state diagrams, message-passing sequence diagrams, algorithm flowcharts, parse/derivation trees, and UML class diagrams. Use whenever a process, structure, or automaton is clearer as a picture than as prose.
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: course-agents
  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I keep diagrams consistent and give a ready template per diagram type so
course agents don't have to invent Mermaid syntax from scratch each time.

## When to use me

Any time a topic is fundamentally about states, transitions, message flow,
tree structure, or class relationships — these render natively in Markdown
viewers/OpenCode and are far clearer than a paragraph describing the same
thing.

## Automata / Turing machines (Computability Theory)

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> q0
  q0 --> q1: 0
  q1 --> q1: 0
  q1 --> q2: 1
  q2 --> [*]
```

## Message passing / distributed algorithms (Parallel & Distributed)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P1
  participant P2
  participant P3
  P1->>P2: REQUEST(ts=3)
  P1->>P3: REQUEST(ts=3)
  P2-->>P1: REPLY
  P3-->>P1: REPLY
  Note over P1: enters critical section
```

## Algorithm flow / decision procedures (any course)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Start] --> B{Condition?}
  B -- yes --> C[Do X]
  B -- no --> D[Do Y]
  C --> E[End]
  D --> E
```

## Parse trees / derivations (Syntax & Semantics)

```mermaid
graph TD
  E1["E"] --> E2["E"]
  E1 --> Plus["+"]
  E1 --> T1["T"]
  E2 --> T2["T"]
  T2 --> id1["id"]
  T1 --> id2["id"]
```

## Class relationships (OOP in C++)

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class Shape {
    <<abstract>>
    +area() double
  }
  class Circle {
    -radius: double
    +area() double
  }
  Shape <|-- Circle
```

## Search / game trees (AI)

```mermaid
graph TD
  Root((Root, MAX)) --> A((A, MIN))
  Root --> B((B, MIN))
  A --> A1["3"]
  A --> A2["5"]
  B --> B1["2"]
  B --> B2["9"]
```

## Rules

- Keep diagrams small and single-purpose — one diagram per concept, not one
  giant diagram trying to show a whole lecture.
- Always caption a diagram with a one-line sentence explaining what to read
  off of it.
- For automata, label every transition with its input symbol; for sequence
  diagrams, label every message with what it actually carries (not just
  "message 1").
- If a diagram is a direct redraw of a slide figure, note that in the caption
  ("redrawn from slide 7") so the student can compare against the original.

name: flashcard-generator
description: Generate spaced-repetition flashcards (Q/A pairs, Anki-importable CSV) from an existing notes.md or sheet solutions. Use when the student asks for flashcards, wants to "drill" a lecture, or before Anki-style spaced-repetition review.

## What I do

I turn already-written lecture notes into atomic recall-testing flashcards,
in both a human-readable Markdown form and an Anki-CSV form.

## When to use me

- On request: "make flashcards for lecture 4", "turn the ring theory unit into
  cards I can drill".
- Run after `lecture-notes-writer` (or `summary-generator`) has produced
  content to draw from — don't invent flashcards from the raw PDF directly,
  since the notes have already done the work of identifying what's important.

## Output location & naming

- `level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/flashcards.md` — human-readable.
- `level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/flashcards.csv` — two columns,
  `front,back`, no header row, ready for Anki's "Basic" note type import.

## Card-writing rules

- **Atomic**: one fact, one definition, or one small step per card. If a
  concept needs three things memorized, that's three cards, not one card with
  a three-part answer.
- **Active recall phrasing**: the front is a question or a fill-in-the-blank,
  never a statement to passively re-read. "What does the Halting Problem
  reduce _from_ in the standard undecidability proof?" not "The Halting
  Problem reduces from...".
- **Cover the whole hierarchy**: definitions, theorem statements, "when to use
  which algorithm/technique" decision cards, and worked-example-style cards
  ("what's the first step in reducing A to B?").
- **No ambiguous answers**: avoid fronts with more than one reasonable
  correct-sounding answer; if a term is overloaded across courses, name the
  course/context on the front.
- **Math/code on cards**: keep LaTeX/code short enough to read in a flashcard
  UI — one formula or one short snippet, not a derivation.
- Tag each card's source lecture in the Markdown version (not the CSV) so the
  student can trace a card back to the notes: `<!-- source: lecture-04 -->`.

## Markdown format

```markdown
## Lecture NN — <topic>

**Q:** <question>
**A:** <answer>

**Q:** <question>
**A:** <answer>
```

## CSV format

```csv
"<question, commas inside must stay quoted>","<answer>"
```

name: lecture-notes-writer
description: Turn extracted lecture/sheet text into a rich, self-contained Markdown explanation file following the study-system's shared notes template (TL;DR, full explanation, worked examples, glossary, practice questions, cheat-sheet). Every level-04 course agent uses this for every lecture/sheet it explains.
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: course-agents
  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I define the one shared shape that every course agent's lecture notes must
follow, so notes for Computability Theory and notes for OOP in C++ look and
navigate the same way even though the content is totally different. A course
agent supplies the domain expertise; this skill supplies the structure and the
bar for depth.

## When to use me

Whenever a course agent is asked to "explain", "write notes for", or "break
down" a lecture or sheet PDF. Run `pdf-ocr` first if the text isn't already
extracted this session.

## The rule that matters most

**Do not paraphrase slide bullets. Reconstruct the reasoning the lecturer
compressed or skipped.** Slides are a compressed pointer to a 50-minute
explanation; your job is to expand each pointer back into the full
explanation — the "why", the intuition, the derivation, the edge case — not to
reformat the bullets with nicer punctuation. If a slide just states a theorem,
you give the proof or at least the proof sketch. If a slide shows a code
snippet, you explain what every line does and why it's written that way.

## Output location & naming

For `level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.pdf`, write:
`level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/notes.md`

For `level-04/semester-01/<course>/sheets/sheet-NN/sheet-NN.pdf`, use the same template but title
it "Sheet NN — Worked Solutions" and put every sub-question's full worked
solution under "Full Detailed Explanation" instead of lecture topics; write to
`level-04/semester-01/<course>/sheets/sheet-NN/solved.md`.

## Template

```markdown
---
course: <course display name>
unit: lecture-NN | sheet-NN
source: lecture-NN/lecture-NN.pdf
generated: <date>
---

# Lecture NN — <topic title>

## TL;DR
- 3-6 bullets: the absolute must-remember takeaways, written so that reading
  only this section before an exam still gives real signal.

## Where this fits
- One or two sentences connecting this lecture to the previous one and to the
  course's overall arc. Note any prerequisite lecture/topic explicitly.

## Learning objectives
- What you should be able to *do* after this lecture (derive X, apply Y to a
  new instance, distinguish A from B), not just "understand Z".

## Full detailed explanation
For each topic on the slides, in order, write a subsection with:
- **Intuition first** — the plain-language idea before any formalism.
- **Formal definition/statement** — precise, using the `math-notation` skill's
  conventions where relevant.
- **Why it's true / how it works** — derivation, proof, or mechanism, not just
  the result. If the lecturer skipped a step, fill it in.
- **Worked example** — a concrete instance carried through step by step, with
  every intermediate step shown (no "it follows that" jumps).
- **Common pitfalls** — the mistake students actually make here.
Use a `###` subsection per topic. Insert a Mermaid diagram (via the
`diagram-generator` skill) anywhere a process, automaton, tree, or pipeline is
easier to see than to read.

## Key definitions & theorems
A Markdown table: | Term | Precise statement | Plain-English meaning |

## Connections
- Bullet links to other lectures/courses this builds on or feeds into
  (e.g. "the pumping lemma here is what Computability Theory Lecture 6 relies
  on"). Use `[[relative/path.md]]`-style links where the target file exists.

## Quick self-check
3-6 short questions with the answer collapsed under a `<details>` block, so
the student can test recall before opening the full quiz/flashcards.

## One-page cheat-sheet
The absolute condensed version: definitions, formulas, and decision rules only,
formatted for a last-minute re-read. (If this is getting long, generate it as
a separate file instead — see the `summary-generator` skill.)

## Source reference
- Slide/page numbers each subsection was drawn from, so the student can go
  back to the original PDF for anything this file compresses too much.
```

## Depth calibration

- Go deep enough that the student could reconstruct the lecture from these
  notes alone without rewatching it — that's the bar, not "cover the slide
  titles."
- Every formula gets a sentence saying where it comes from or what it means,
  never a bare equation.
- Every code snippet gets explained line-by-line for anything non-obvious.
- Flag, explicitly, anything the source PDF states without justification —
  "the slides assert this without proof; here's the standard argument" — so
  the student can tell lecture content apart from your added scaffolding.

name: math-notation
description: House style for writing mathematical notation in Markdown (LaTeX delimiters, symbol conventions per course — group/ring/field theory, automata and Turing machine tuples, Big-O, formal grammars, logic). Use whenever any study-system agent writes a formula, theorem, or formal definition.
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: course-agents
  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I keep math notation consistent across every course's notes so formulas render
correctly and mean the same thing everywhere they're used.

## Delimiters

- Inline math: `$...$` — e.g. `$a \equiv b \pmod{n}$`.
- Display math: `$$...$$` on its own line for anything with fractions, sums,
  multi-line derivations, or matrix/tuple notation.
- Never leave a formula as plain-text pseudo-math (`a^2 + b^2 = c^2` typed with
  `^` outside `$...$`) — always wrap it.
- For a multi-step derivation, use an `aligned` block so `=` signs line up:

```
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(n) &= 2f(n/2) + n \\
     &= 4f(n/4) + 2n \\
     &= \dots \\
     &= n \log n
\end{aligned}
$$
```

## Per-course symbol conventions

**Abstract Math (Groups/Rings/Fields)**

- Groups: $(G, \cdot)$ or $(G, +)$; identity $e$ (or $0$ additively);
  subgroup $H \le G$; normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$; quotient
  $G/N$; order $|G|$, $\mathrm{ord}(g)$; homomorphism $\varphi: G \to H$;
  kernel $\ker\varphi$.
- Rings: $(R, +, \cdot)$; ideal $I \trianglelefteq R$; quotient ring $R/I$;
  units $R^\times$.
- Fields: $\mathbb{F}_q$ or $GF(q)$ for a finite field of order $q$; field
  extension $\mathbb{F} \subseteq \mathbb{K}$, written $\mathbb{K}/\mathbb{F}$.

**Computability Theory**

- A Turing machine as the 7-tuple
  $M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{accept}, q_{reject})$; always define
  every symbol the first time a TM appears in a file.
- Languages: $L(M)$; decidable class often written informally as "R" or
  "decidable", recognizable as "RE"/"recognizable" — say which convention the
  course uses and stick to it in that file.
- Reductions: $A \le_m B$ (many-one/mapping reduction).

**Syntax & Semantics**

- Grammar $G = (N, \Sigma, P, S)$; production $A \to \alpha$.
- Operational semantics rules as inference rules:

```
$$
\dfrac{e_1 \Downarrow v_1 \qquad e_2 \Downarrow v_2}{e_1 + e_2 \Downarrow v_1 + v_2}
$$
```

**Parallel & Distributed Processing**

- Big-O family: $O(\cdot)$, $\Omega(\cdot)$, $\Theta(\cdot)$.
- Speedup $S(p) = T_1 / T_p$; Amdahl's law
  $S(p) = \dfrac{1}{(1-f) + f/p}$ — always state what $f$ means in that file.

**AI**

- Search: state $s$, action $a$, path cost $g(n)$, heuristic $h(n)$,
  evaluation $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$.
- Probability/logic as standard: $P(A \mid B)$, $\forall$, $\exists$,
  $\models$.

## General rules

- Define every symbol on first use in a file — don't assume the reader
  remembers a convention from a different lecture.
- Prefer a small glossary table (see `lecture-notes-writer`'s "Key
  definitions" section) over re-explaining notation inline every time.
- If OCR produced a formula you're not fully confident in (see `pdf-ocr`),
  say so rather than silently presenting a guess as certain.

name: pdf-ocr
description: Extract clean text from lecture/sheet PDFs under level-04 (including scanned slides, image-heavy decks, and mixed Arabic/English pages) using pdftotext, pdftoppm and tesseract. Use before writing notes whenever a PDF's text layer is missing, garbled, or the slides are equation/diagram-heavy.
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: course-agents
  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I turn a lecture/sheet PDF into text a course agent can actually read and reason
about, and I flag the parts that OCR cannot be trusted on (equations, diagrams,
hand-drawn figures) so those get transcribed by eye instead of guessed at.

## When to use me

- Any time a course agent is asked to explain `lecture-NN.pdf` or `sheet-NN.pdf`
  and hasn't already extracted its text this session.
- Any time direct extraction returns near-empty or clearly garbled output
  (common for scanned slides, slides exported as flattened images, or
  photographed whiteboards).

## Procedure

**0. Ensure the per-lecture folder exists and the PDF is inside it.**

```bash
mkdir -p "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN"
mv "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN.pdf" \
   "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/" 2>/dev/null || true
```

If the PDF is already inside `lectures/lecture-NN/`, the `mv` is a no-op.
Sheets follow the same pattern: `sheets/sheet-NN/sheet-NN.pdf`.

**1. Try direct text extraction first (fast, exact, no OCR errors).**

```bash
pdftotext -layout "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.pdf" \
               "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.raw.txt"
wc -w "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.raw.txt"
```

`-layout` preserves column/table positioning, which matters for slides with
side-by-side diagrams+bullets or code blocks.

**2. Judge the quality before trusting it.**

Red flags that mean you need OCR instead:

- Word count is near zero relative to the number of pages.
- Output is dominated by single characters, `(cid:NN)` tokens, or repeated
  garbage symbols (classic sign of a custom/embedded font with no text layer).
- Math-heavy lines look like scrambled symbol soup.

**3. Fallback: rasterize pages, then OCR each page.**

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/ocr/lecture-NN
pdftoppm -r 300 -png "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.pdf" /tmp/ocr/lecture-NN/page
for f in /tmp/ocr/lecture-NN/page-*.png; do
  tesseract "$f" "${f%.png}" --psm 6
done
cat /tmp/ocr/lecture-NN/page-*.txt > "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.raw.txt"
```

- `--psm 6` ("assume a uniform block of text") is a good default for slide
  bullets; try `--psm 4` for multi-column slides.
- If tools are missing, install them once: `apt-get install -y poppler-utils tesseract-ocr`
  (or `tesseract-ocr-ara` if Arabic text appears on slides, then run
  `tesseract "$f" "${f%.png}" -l eng+ara --psm 6`).

**4. Never trust OCR for math, diagrams, or hand-drawn figures.**

Tesseract regularly mangles subscripts, Greek letters, summation/product
signs, and arrows. For any slide containing formulas, automata diagrams,
circuit/pipeline diagrams, or graphs:

- Open the rasterized page image directly with the `view` tool and read it
  visually.
- Transcribe the math by hand into proper LaTeX (see the `math-notation`
  skill) rather than copying OCR output.
- Redraw diagrams as Mermaid (see the `diagram-generator` skill) instead of
  describing a mangled OCR dump of a picture.

**5. Use the raw extraction, then clean up.**

Read the `.raw.txt` file to produce structured notes via `lecture-notes-writer`,
then **delete all temporary artifacts** once the notes file is written:

```bash
rm -f "level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/lecture-NN.raw.txt"
rm -rf /tmp/ocr/lecture-NN
```

Never hand `.raw.txt` to the student as-is — it always gets rewritten into the
structured notes format. The raw file is a working artifact, not a deliverable.

## Common pitfalls

- Running OCR on a PDF that already had a perfectly good text layer (slow and
  worse quality than direct extraction — always try `pdftotext` first).
- Trusting OCR'd numbers/formulas verbatim in a math-heavy course — always
  cross-check against the rasterized image.
- Forgetting `-layout`, which causes tables and two-column slides to interleave
  into nonsense.
- Silently dropping pages that failed OCR — report which page numbers were
  unreadable so the student knows to check the original PDF.

name: quiz-generator
description: Generate a practice quiz (mixed multiple-choice and short-answer/problem questions, with a full answer key) from an existing notes.md or a whole course unit. Use when the student asks to be quizzed, wants exam practice, or asks to "test me" on a lecture or topic.
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode

  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I write exam-style practice questions that test understanding and problem
solving, not just recall (recall is what `flashcard-generator` is for), plus a
complete answer key with reasoning.

## When to use me

- On request: "quiz me on lecture 6", "give me a practice exam for the ring
  theory unit", "test me like the midterm would".
- Draw from `notes.md` in the lecture folder (and the sheet solutions, if a sheet exists
  for the same topic) rather than re-deriving from the raw PDF.

## Output location & naming

`level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/quiz.md` for a single lecture, or
`level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/unit-quiz-<topic>.md` when asked to cover several lectures.

## Question design

- **Mix formats**: multiple-choice for definitions/discrimination between
  similar concepts, short-answer for "state and justify", and full
  problem/derivation questions for anything computational (build a parse
  table, run a reduction, trace an algorithm, prove a small claim).
- **Difficulty tiers**: label each question Easy / Medium / Hard, and include
  at least one Hard question per major topic that requires combining two
  ideas from the lecture, not just restating one.
- **Multiple-choice discipline**: exactly one correct option, distractors must
  be genuinely plausible mistakes (a common misconception, an off-by-one, a
  confusion with a similar theorem) — never an obviously silly option just to
  fill a slot.
- **Match the course's actual exam style** where known (e.g. Abstract Math and
  Computability Theory lean toward "state and prove/derive"; OOP in C++ and AI
  lean toward "trace this code" / "design this algorithm"; Parallel &
  Distributed and Syntax & Semantics mix both).

## Answer key format

Put the key in its own `## Answer Key` section at the end (not inline after
each question, so it can double as a closed-book test):

```markdown
**Q3.** <short restated answer, then the full reasoning — not just the letter
or the final number>
```

Every answer must show _why_, not just _what_, so a wrong guess still teaches
something when the student checks it.

name: summary-generator
description: Condense an already-written notes.md into a one-page, last-minute-review summary or exam cheat-sheet. Use after lecture-notes-writer has produced full notes, or when the student explicitly asks for a shorter version / cheat-sheet / TL;DR of a lecture, sheet, or whole course.
license: MIT

metadata:
  audience: course-agents
  domain: study-system
---

## What I do

I compress full lecture notes down to what fits on one screen without losing
anything a student would actually need in the last hour before an exam.

## When to use me

- Right after `lecture-notes-writer` finishes a lecture, if the student wants
  a standalone condensed file (common when the full notes run long).
- On request: "summarize lecture 5", "give me a cheat sheet for the whole
  ring theory unit", "condense sheet 3's solutions".
- Building a per-course master cheat-sheet by concatenating per-lecture
  summaries before an exam.

## Output location & naming

Single lecture: `level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/lecture-NN/summary.md`
Whole-unit/course: `level-04/semester-01/<course>/lectures/course-cheatsheet.md` (append a new
`## Lecture NN` section each time you're asked to extend it, don't overwrite
previous lectures' sections).

## Compression rules

- Start from the **existing** `notes.md` in the lecture folder if it exists — don't
  re-derive from the raw PDF, that's `lecture-notes-writer`'s job and
  duplicating it wastes the depth already captured.
- Keep: every definition, every formula, every named theorem/algorithm,
  decision rules ("use X when Y, use Z when W"), and the one-line intuition
  for each — the compressed memory hook, not the full explanation.
- Cut: intuition build-up, full proofs/derivations (keep proof *technique
  name* only, e.g. "proof by diagonalization"), narrative connective tissue,
  and the source-reference section.
- Format as dense bullets and tables, not paragraphs. Bold every term being
  defined. One line per fact where at all possible.
- Preserve any Mermaid diagram from the source notes that captures a whole
  process in one glance (state diagrams, decision flowcharts) — these compress
  better than prose.
- Target length: short enough to review in under 5 minutes per lecture.

## Course-level cheat-sheet assembly

When asked for a whole-course cheat-sheet, organize by topic (not
chronologically by lecture) if topics recur across lectures — e.g. group every
mention of "mutual exclusion algorithms" together even if it was taught across
two lectures. Add a short "how topics connect" map at the top.

# College

Level-04 lecture notes, flashcards, quizzes, and summaries — generated and maintained by [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) agents.

## Courses

| Course                                        | Folder                                |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Parallel and Distributed Processing           | `level-04/semester-01/parallel/`      |
| Syntax and Semantics of Programming Languages | `level-04/semester-01/syntax/`        |
| Artificial Intelligence                       | `level-04/semester-01/ai/`            |
| Computability Theory                          | `level-04/semester-01/computability/` |
| Object-Oriented Programming in C++            | `level-04/semester-01/oop/`           |
| Abstract Mathematics                          | `level-04/semester-01/math/`          |

## File structure

Each lecture and sheet gets its own folder:

```
lectures/
  lecture-01/
    lecture-01.pdf        # source PDF from the lecturer
    notes.md              # full detailed notes
    summary.md            # one-page cheat sheet
    flashcards.md         # Q/A pairs for spaced repetition
    flashcards.csv        # Anki-importable version
    quiz.md               # practice exam with answer key

sheets/
  sheet-01/
    sheet-01.pdf
    solved.md             # worked solutions
```

Course-level files sit in the course root:

```
parallel/
  course-cheatsheet.md    # master cheat sheet (all lectures combined)
  unit-quiz-<topic>.md    # multi-lecture practice quizzes
```

## How it works

This repo uses OpenCode with custom **skills** and **agents** (in `.opencode/`) to automate note generation:

1. A lecture PDF is placed in `lectures/` (or `sheets/`).
2. The course agent extracts text via `pdf-ocr` (pdftotext / tesseract).
3. `lecture-notes-writer` produces structured notes with definitions, proofs, examples, and diagrams.
4. `summary-generator`, `flashcard-generator`, and `quiz-generator` produce additional study materials from the notes.

### Skills

| Skill                  | Purpose                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pdf-ocr`              | Extract text from PDFs (direct extraction or OCR fallback)  |
| `lecture-notes-writer` | Write full structured lecture notes                         |
| `summary-generator`    | Compress notes into a one-page cheat sheet                  |
| `flashcard-generator`  | Generate Anki-compatible flashcards                         |
| `quiz-generator`       | Generate practice quizzes with answer keys                  |
| `math-notation`        | LaTeX conventions across all courses                        |
| `diagram-generator`    | Mermaid diagram templates (automata, sequences, flowcharts) |

### Agents

| Agent                  | Course                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `parallel-distributed` | Parallel and Distributed Processing           |
| `syntax-semantics`     | Syntax and Semantics of Programming Languages |
| `computability`        | Computability Theory                          |

Dependencies are installed automatically by the agents when needed.

## 1. All Definitions (one line each)

### Programs & processes
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sequential program** $S$ | Single instruction stream on one processor; correctness = Hoare triple $\{p\}\;S\;\{q\}$. |
| **Partial correctness** | *If* $S$ terminates on valid input, output satisfies $q$. (Ignores termination.) |
| **Total correctness** | Partial correctness **+** $S$ always terminates. |
| **Sequential process** | Dynamic execution: ordered operations $o_1,o_2,\dots$; next op starts only after previous completes. |
| **Parallel/concurrent program** | Decomposition into tasks (each internally sequential) run simultaneously. |
| **Synchronous execution** | Caller waits for each op → forces sequential order. |
| **Asynchronous execution** | Ops overlap/interleave; no waiting between processes. |

### Architectures (the course's central axis)
| | **Shared memory** | **Distributed memory** |
|---|---|---|
| Address space | one **global** | **private** per processor |
| Communication | read/write shared RAM | **message passing** over network |
| Sync burden | programmer's (critical sections) | explicit messages |
| Failure | single machine | **separate failure domains** |
| Maps to | pthreads / OpenMP | MPI |

### Correctness of concurrent programs
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Correctness of a concurrent program** | Each task is correct **and** the global properties hold: **mutual exclusion**, **deadlock freedom** (safety) and **liveness/no starvation**. |
| **Safety property** | "**Nothing bad happens**": mutual exclusion + freedom from deadlock. |
| **Liveness property** | "**Something good eventually happens**": every requesting process eventually gets the resource. |
| **Mutual exclusion** | At any time, no resource is used by more than one process. |
| **Deadlock** | Two+ processes permanently blocked, **each waiting on the other**. |
| **Starvation** | A process waits forever because the resource is *never allocated to it* (no circular wait required). |
| **Race condition** | Outcome depends on unpredictable interleaving of non-atomic shared access. |

### Critical section & semaphores
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Critical section (CS)** | The fragment of a process that **uses a shared resource**; requirement: ≤1 task in its CS at a time. |
| **Critical section problem** | A group of processes compete for a resource where only one may have access at a time (shared vars, DB records, files, printers). |
| **Semaphore** $s=(w,q)$ | $w\in\mathbb{N}_0$ = counter; $q$ = set/**FIFO queue** of tasks blocked on $s$. |
| **Binary semaphore** | $w\in\{0,1\}$ (1 = free, 0 = used) → **mutual exclusion** (lock). |
| **General semaphore** | $w\in\mathbb{N}_0$ → **counting / condition synchronisation**. |
| **`wait(s)`** (atomic) | if $w>0$ then $w{:=}w-1$; else **block** task, add to $q$. |
| **`signal(s)`** (atomic) | if $q\neq\emptyset$ then unblock one task; else $w{:=}w+1$. |
| **Condition synchronisation** | Waiting for an **event/state** (data available) rather than for a lock. |
| **Producer–consumer problem** | Producer generates data → buffer → consumer retrieves & processes. |

### Higher-level patterns
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Bounded buffer** | Fixed cyclic array of size $n$; index wraps as `(idx+1) mod n`. |
| **Circular wait** | Each holder waits on a resource held by the next, forming a cycle (1 of 4 deadlock conditions). |
| **Fork (pattern)** | One task splits into $k\ge2$ concurrent subtasks (fan-out). |
| **Join (pattern)** | Subtasks sync back to one continuation = a **barrier** (fan-in). |
| **Reader access condition** | A reader may access iff **no writer is currently inside**. |
| **Writer access condition** | A writer may access iff **no reader and no writer is inside** (fully exclusive). |
| **Monitor** | Construct encapsulating **private shared data + procedures + condition variables**; **≤1 process active inside at a time** (auto mutual exclusion). |
| **Condition variable** | FIFO queue of blocked processes with **no stored value**; `signal` with no waiter is **lost**. |
| **Lost wakeup** | A `signal` with no waiter has no effect → must re-check a state variable. |

## 2. Quick-reference Tables

### 2.1 Bounded vs Unbounded buffer — advantages / disadvantages (high-yield!)
| | **Unbounded buffer** | **Bounded buffer** |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | `array(0..∞)`, `in,out:=0`, never wraps | `array(0..n-1)`, `in:=(in+1) mod n` |
| Semaphores | **1** (`nonempty := (0,∅)`) | **2** (`nonempty := (0,∅)`, `nonfull := (n,∅)`) |
| Producer ever blocks? | **No** (buffer never full) | **Yes** — on `wait(nonfull)` when full |
| **Advantages** | Simple; producer never delayed | Fixed memory; **backpressure/flow control**; realistic; predictable resource use |
| **Disadvantages** | Memory grows → **overflow/exhaustion** if producer faster; theoretical only | More state; producer latency under load; needs cyclic indices |
| Invariant | `nonempty.w = #items` | `nonempty.w + nonfull.w = n` |

### 2.2 Semaphore `wait` / `signal` (must be ATOMIC)
```text
wait(s):   if s.w > 0 then s.w := s.w - 1        else suspend task; add to s.q
signal(s): if s.q ≠ ∅  then remove one task, resume it   else s.w := s.w + 1
```
> **Without atomicity:** two tasks both read $s.w=1$, both decrement, both enter the CS → **mutual exclusion violated** (race).

### 2.3 Condition variables vs Semaphores (L03 punchline)
| Aspect | Condition variable | Semaphore |
|---|---|---|
| Value | **none** | integer counter |
| Counting | cannot count ops | counts `wait`/`signal` |
| Wait | block + insert in FIFO queue (+ **release monitor lock**) | decrement; block if <0 |
| Signal | wake one waiter, **else lost** | increment; wake if waiting |

### 2.4 Two semaphore roles (do not confuse)
| | Mutual exclusion | Condition sync |
|---|---|---|
| Semaphore | **binary**, $w\in\{0,1\}$ | **general**, $w\in\mathbb{N}_0$ |
| Blocks when | resource busy ($w=0$) | event not ready (e.g. buffer empty) |
| Resumes when | holder `signal`s | producer/other task `signal`s |

### 2.5 Decision rules ("use X when Y")
- One-at-a-time resource → **binary semaphore** around the CS.
- Wait for an event/state → **general semaphore** (condition sync).
- Producer *must* be throttled / finite memory → **bounded buffer** (+`nonfull`).
- Many readers, few writers, must not starve writers → **no-starvation Readers–Writers**.
- Want mutual exclusion with **no** manual `wait`/`signal` bookkeeping → **monitor**.
- 5 philosophers deadlock → break circular wait with a **seat semaphore (`up_to_4`)**.

## 3. All Problem Code

### 3.1 Critical Section — mutual exclusion for $n$ tasks
```text
s: semaphore := (1, ∅);         -- binary = free

task Ti (i = 1..n):
    wait(s);                    -- acquire
        critical section        -- use shared resource
    signal(s);                  -- release
```
- **Mutual-exclusion proof:** `wait` is atomic ⇒ only one task can see $w=1$ and decrement it to 0; all others block on $q$.
- **Deadlock-freedom proof (contradiction):** if two tasks were both blocked, then $w=0$ and both in $q$; but $w=0$ means one already decremented from 1 ⇒ only one was inside ⇒ contradiction. ∎
- **Liveness:** FIFO $q$ ⇒ no starvation.

### 3.2 Producer–Consumer — **UNBOUNDED** buffer (L01)
```text
buffer: array(0..∞) of data_type;
in, out: natural := 0;
nonempty: semaphore := (0, ∅);          -- general: # items in buffer

task Producer:                          task Consumer:
  loop                                    loop
    Produce data;                           wait(nonempty);      -- block if empty
    buffer(in) := data;                     data := buffer(out);
    in := in + 1;                           out := out + 1;
    signal(nonempty);                       Consume data;
  end loop                                end loop
```
- Consumer with $w=0$ → **blocks** on `nonempty.q` until producer signals (condition sync).
- **Failure without `nonempty`:** consumer reads `buffer(out)` — **stale/uninitialised garbage**.
- **Disadvantage:** unbounded → **memory exhaustion** if producer faster.

### 3.3 Producer–Consumer — **BOUNDED** buffer (L02) ★
```text
buffer: array(0..n-1) of data_type;         -- cyclic
in, out: natural := 0;
nonempty: semaphore := (0, ∅);              -- # items
nonfull : semaphore := (n, ∅);              -- # free slots

task Producer:                              task Consumer:
  loop                                        loop
    Produce data;                               wait(nonempty);       -- block if empty
    wait(nonfull);         -- block if full     data := buffer(out);
    buffer(in) := data;                         out := (out + 1) mod n;
    in := (in + 1) mod n;                       signal(nonfull);      -- 1 more free slot
    signal(nonempty);      -- 1 more item       Consume data;
  end loop                                    end loop
```
- **Invariant:** `nonempty.w + nonfull.w = n` (items + free slots = capacity).
- `wait(nonfull)` ⇒ never insert into a full buffer (count ≤ n).
- `wait(nonempty)` ⇒ never retrieve from an empty buffer (count ≥ 0).
- Producer and consumer wait on **different** semaphores ⇒ **no circular wait, no deadlock**.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant B as Cyclic Buffer (size n)
    participant C as Consumer
    Note over B: in=0,out=0,nonempty=0,nonfull=n
    P->>B: wait(nonfull); buffer(in):=data; in=(in+1)mod n; signal(nonempty)
    C->>B: wait(nonempty); data:=buffer(out); out=(out+1)mod n; signal(nonfull)
    Note over B: n inserts with no consume ⇒ nonfull=0 ⇒ producer blocks
```

### 3.4 Dining Philosophers (L02)
5 philosophers, 5 forks; philosopher $i$ needs left fork $i$ and right fork $(i+1)\bmod 5$; each fork a **binary semaphore**.

**Naive (deadlock-prone) — left then right:**
```text
fork: array(0..4) of semaphore := (1, ∅);
task Philosopher_i:
  loop
    Think;
    wait(fork(i));              -- LEFT
    wait(fork((i+1) mod 5));    -- RIGHT
    Eat;
    signal(fork(i));
    signal(fork((i+1) mod 5));
  end loop
```
**Bug — circular wait:** all 5 grab their left fork, each waits for a right fork held by a neighbour ⇒ waits-for cycle $P_0\to P_1\to P_2\to P_3\to P_4\to P_0$ ⇒ **deadlock** (and possible starvation).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P0["P0 holds F0, wants F1"] --> P1["P1 holds F1, wants F2"]
    P1 --> P2["P2 holds F2, wants F3"]
    P2 --> P3["P3 holds F3, wants F4"]
    P3 --> P4["P4 holds F4, wants F0"]
    P4 --> P0
```

**Fixed — seat semaphore `up_to_4` (breaks circular wait):**
```text
up_to_4: semaphore := (4, ∅);       -- at most 4 seated
task Philosopher_i:
  loop
    Think;
    wait(up_to_4);              -- take a seat (blocks if 4 already seated)
    wait(fork(i));
    wait(fork((i+1) mod 5));
    Eat;
    signal(fork(i));
    signal(fork((i+1) mod 5));
    signal(up_to_4);            -- release seat LAST
  end loop
```
- **Deadlock-free:** a 5-cycle needs all 5 seated; with ≤4 seated, one philosopher always gets both forks.
- **Starvation-free:** if $i$ blocked forever on `up_to_4`, then 4 are seated; one of them eats and leaves → `up_to_4.w>0` → $i$ admitted. Contradiction. ∎
- **Max eating concurrency:** $\lfloor 5/2\rfloor = 2$ philosophers.

C/pthreads equivalence (scaffolding):
```c
sem_t fork_[5], up_to_4;                       // init 1 each, up_to_4 init 4
int left = i, right = (i+1) % 5;
sem_wait(&up_to_4);
sem_wait(&fork_[left]);  sem_wait(&fork_[right]);
eat(i);
sem_post(&fork_[left]);  sem_post(&fork_[right]);  sem_post(&up_to_4);
```

### 3.5 Readers–Writers (L03)
**Access rules:** reader iff no writer *inside*; writer iff no reader and no writer *inside*.

**First solution — reader-priority (STARVES WRITERS):**
```text
s: semaphore := (1, ∅);             -- guards no_of_readers
access: semaphore := (1, ∅);        -- guards the database
no_of_readers: natural := 0;

reader:                             writer:
  loop                                loop
    wait(s);                            wait(access);
    no_of_readers := no_of_readers+1;   Write data;
    if no_of_readers = 1 then           signal(access);
       wait(access);                end loop
    end if;
    signal(s);
    Read data;
    wait(s);
    no_of_readers := no_of_readers-1;
    if no_of_readers = 0 then
       signal(access);
    end if;
    signal(s);
  end loop
```
- **Reader-priority:** first reader takes `access`; last reader releases it; middle readers only touch `s` → many readers concurrently.
- **Writer starvation:** if readers keep arriving, `no_of_readers` never hits 0 ⇒ `signal(access)` never runs ⇒ `access` never released ⇒ writers block **forever** (liveness failure, *not* deadlock).

**Correct solution — no starvation (writer-priority on arrival):**
```text
s := (1,∅);  reading_allowed := (0,∅);  writing_allowed := (0,∅);
nr, nw  := 0;   -- USING readers / writers
nwr,nww := 0;   -- WAITING readers / writers

reader:                                  writer:
  wait(s);                                 wait(s);
  if nw > 0 then                           if nr>0 or nw>0 then
     nwr := nwr+1;  signal(s);                nww := nww+1;  signal(s);
     wait(reading_allowed);                   wait(writing_allowed);
  end if;                                  end if;
  nr := nr+1;                              nw := nw+1;  signal(s);
  if nwr>0 then nwr:=nwr-1; signal(reading_allowed);
  else signal(s); end if;                  Write data;
  Read data;                               wait(s);  nw := nw-1;
  wait(s); nr := nr-1;                     if nwr>0 then nwr:=nwr-1; signal(reading_allowed);
  if nr=0 and nww>0 then                       else if nww>0 then nww:=nww-1; signal(writing_allowed);
     nww:=nww-1; signal(writing_allowed);      else signal(s); end if;
  else signal(s); end if;
```
- **Rule 1:** new reader blocked if a writer *waits* → `wait(reading_allowed)` (removes writer starvation).
- **Rule 2:** last reader (`nr=0`, `nww>0`) → `signal(writing_allowed)`.
- **Rule 3:** writer finishes → wake waiting readers first, else a writer.
- **Baton passing:** the waker does **not** `signal(s)`; the woken process releases `s`.
- Variants: **reader-priority** (writers starve) · **writer-priority** · **no-starvation/fair** (this).

### 3.6 Producer–Consumer with a **Monitor** (L03)
```text
monitor Producer_Consumer is
  buffer: array(0..n-1) of data_type;
  in, out, counter: natural := 0;          -- counter = # items
  nonempty, nonfull: condition;

  procedure put(d) is
    if counter = n then wait(nonfull); end if;   -- full ⇒ wait space
    buffer(in) := d;  in := (in+1) mod n;
    counter := counter + 1;
    signal(nonempty);                            -- data available
  end put;

  procedure get(d) is
    if counter = 0 then wait(nonempty); end if;  -- empty ⇒ wait data
    d := buffer(out);  out := (out+1) mod n;
    counter := counter - 1;
    signal(nonfull);                             -- space available
  end get;
end Producer_Consumer;
```
- Callers just: `Producer_Consumer.put(data)` / `Producer_Consumer.get(data)` — **no full/empty checks**.
- Monitor gives mutual exclusion automatically; condition variables handle full/empty.
- POSIX: monitor ≈ `pthread_mutex_t` + `pthread_cond_t`; `pthread_cond_wait(&cv,&m)` **atomically releases** the mutex; use `while`, not `if`.

### 3.7 Fork–Join (L02)
- **Fork** = one task splits into $k\ge2$ concurrent subtasks; **Join** = barrier, all subtasks must finish before the continuation runs.
- Segment time = $\max(t_B,t_C)$, **not** $t_B+t_C$; imbalance makes the shorter branch idle (load-imbalance / Amdahl).
- Dependency $A\to\{B,C\}\to D$ via `S_B,S_C` (init 0) and `done_B,done_C` (init 0):

```text
A: Operations A; signal(S_B); signal(S_C);
B: wait(S_B); Operations B; signal(done_B);
C: wait(S_C); Operations C; signal(done_C);
D: wait(done_B); wait(done_C); Operations D;
```

## 4. Exam Read Q/A  (questions exactly as they appear + model answers)

### Q. What is the correctness of concurrent programs? *(4 Marks)*
Correctness has **two layers**:
1. **Local:** each individual task (a sequential program) is correct — satisfies its Hoare triple $\{p\}\,S\,\{q\}$ (partial + termination = total correctness).
2. **Global:** the **synchronisation properties** hold:
   - **Safety** ("nothing bad happens") — **mutual exclusion** (≤1 process in its critical section) and **freedom from deadlock**.
   - **Liveness** ("something good eventually happens") — every requesting process **eventually gets the resource** (no starvation).
> A concurrent program is correct **iff** every task is correct **and** all global safety + liveness properties hold.

### Q. Define the safety property of concurrent programs. *(3 Marks)*
A **safety property** states that **"nothing bad ever happens"** during execution. For concurrent programs it comprises:
- **Mutual exclusion** — at any time, no resource is used by more than one process.
- **Freedom from deadlock** — no situation where two or more processes can never terminate because each is permanently waiting on the other.
> Intuition: it is a *lower bound* on correctness (a bad state is never reached); it says nothing about progress — that is the job of the **liveness** property.

### Q. What is a critical section, and how can it be solved? *(4 Marks)* *(also asked as 2 Marks)*
- **Critical section (CS):** the fragment of a process (task) that **uses a shared resource** (shared variable, file, DB record, printer) which may be used by **only one process at a time**. Requirement: **at most one task executes its CS at any moment**.
- **The problem:** a group of processes compete for that resource → need mutual exclusion + no deadlock + no starvation.
- **Solution** — three-phase protocol **acquire → use → release**, implemented with a **binary semaphore** $s := (1,\emptyset)$:
```text
wait(s);      -- acquire permission
  critical section
signal(s);    -- release
```
  - `wait` and `signal` are **atomic**, so only one task can decrement $s.w$ from 1 to 0; all others block on the queue (mutual exclusion).
  - Other solutions: **Peterson's algorithm**, **test-and-set** instruction, **semaphores**, **monitors** (all later lectures).

### Q. What are semaphores? *(1 Mark)*
A **semaphore** is a synchronisation primitive $s=(w,q)$: $w$ is a **nonnegative integer counter** and $q$ is a **FIFO set/queue of blocked tasks**. Operations `wait(s)` (decrement, or block) and `signal(s)` (wake a waiter, or increment) are **atomic**. **Binary** semaphores ($w\in\{0,1\}$) give mutual exclusion; **general** semaphores ($w\in\mathbb{N}_0$) give counting/condition synchronisation.

### Q. Give a solution to the producer–consumer problem using an **unbounded** buffer. *(5 or 7 Marks)*
**Data:**
```text
buffer: array(0..∞) of data_type;   in, out := 0;
nonempty: semaphore := (0, ∅);      -- general; counts items present
```
**Producer:** `Produce data; buffer(in):=data; in:=in+1; signal(nonempty);`
**Consumer:** `wait(nonempty); data:=buffer(out); out:=out+1; Consume data;`
**Explanation:** with an unbounded buffer the producer **never blocks**; only the consumer can block. `nonempty` is a **general semaphore** performing **condition synchronisation** — if the buffer is empty ($w=0$) the consumer blocks on `nonempty.q` until the producer's `signal` makes data available. Without `nonempty` the consumer would read uninitialised/stale data.
> **Drawback:** memory grows without bound → **exhaustion** if the producer is faster.

### Q. Give a solution to the producer–consumer problem using a **bounded** buffer and explain why the bounded buffer is better than the unbounded buffer. *(7 Marks)* ★
**Data (cyclic array of size $n$):**
```text
buffer: array(0..n-1) of data_type;   in, out := 0;
nonempty: semaphore := (0, ∅);        -- items present
nonfull : semaphore := (n, ∅);        -- free slots
```
**Producer:** `Produce; wait(nonfull); buffer(in):=data; in:=(in+1) mod n; signal(nonempty);`
**Consumer:** `wait(nonempty); data:=buffer(out); out:=(out+1) mod n; signal(nonfull); Consume;`
**Invariant:** `nonempty.w + nonfull.w = n`.
- `wait(nonfull)` stops insertion into a **full** buffer; `wait(nonempty)` stops retrieval from an **empty** buffer.
- Producer and consumer wait on **different** semaphores ⇒ no circular wait ⇒ no deadlock.

**Why bounded is better than unbounded:**
1. **Finite memory** — bounded uses a fixed $n$ slots; unbounded can grow until it **overflows/exhausts** memory when the producer outpaces the consumer.
2. **Flow control / backpressure** — bounded blocks the producer (`wait(nonfull)`) when full, keeping producer and consumer balanced; unbounded hides overload until it is too late.
3. **Realistic & predictable** — real systems have finite buffers; bounded gives bounded latency and deterministic resource usage.
4. **Reusability** — the cyclic `mod n` index recycles slots forever; unbounded keeps allocating.

### Q. (variant) Distinguish shared-memory and distributed-memory, with adv/disadv.
- **Shared memory:** one global address space; communication = read/write; **adv** fast, simple; **disadv** programmer must synchronise (critical sections), single point of failure.
- **Distributed memory:** private memory per processor; communication = **message passing** over a network; **adv** scalable, fault-isolated, geographically spread; **disadv** slower communication, complex, partial failure (need fault tolerance). Standard failure model: **fail-stop**.

### Q. (likely) Give the Dining Philosophers problem and a deadlock-free solution. *(see §3.4)*
State the naive left-then-right solution deadlocks (circular wait), then add `up_to_4 := (4,∅)`; prove deadlock-freedom and starvation-freedom; note max eating concurrency $=\lfloor 5/2\rfloor=2$.

### Q. (likely) Give the Readers–Writers problem: first solution and why it may starve writers. *(see §3.5)*
State the two access conditions; give the reader-priority solution; explain that if `no_of_readers` never returns to 0, `signal(access)` never executes ⇒ writers starve. Then give the no-starvation solution.

### Q. (likely) What is a monitor and how does it differ from semaphores? *(see §1, §2.3, §3.6)*
Monitor = encapsulated private data + procedures + condition variables with **automatic mutual exclusion** (≤1 active process). Condition variables carry **no value** (signal with no waiter is lost), unlike semaphores which are stateful counters.

## 5. Traps & examiner's gotchas
- **Safety vs liveness:** deadlock = safety failure; starvation = **liveness** failure. Proving one does **not** prove the other.
- **Mutual exclusion vs condition sync:** a semaphore guards a CS (binary) **or** waits for an event (general) — say which.
- **Atomicity of `wait`/`signal`** is *the* reason semaphores work; state it in every proof.
- **Bounded buffer** needs **two** semaphores; **unbounded** needs **one** — a classic exam discriminator.
- **Readers–Writers first solution is "not entirely correct"** despite giving mutual exclusion — it starves writers.
- **Condition variable ≠ semaphore:** `signal` with no waiter is **lost**; state must live in a monitor variable (`counter`).
- **`signal` should be the last statement** in a monitor procedure (condition must still hold at hand-off).
- **Fork–join time = max, not sum** of branch times; imbalance wastes the shorter branch.
- **Dining Philosophers:** releasing the seat (`signal(up_to_4)`) must come **after** releasing both forks.
- **Shared vs distributed:** everything in L01–L03 is shared memory — never talk about "message complexity" here.

## Answer Key

**Q1. B.** Shared-memory = one global address space (read/write directly); distributed-memory = private memories joined by a network (message passing). A reverses the two. C is false — shared memory still needs synchronization (that's the whole critical-section problem). D reverses the failure-domain property (separate failure domains belong to distributed systems).

**Q2. B.** $s=(w,q)$: $w$ is a nonnegative integer (the counter/weight), $q$ is a set (FIFO queue) of blocked tasks. A, C, D are the common misreadings; in particular $w$ is an integer, never a real, and $q$ is never the counter.

**Q3. B.** A binary semaphore is a lock, so it starts **free** = $1$: `(1, ∅)`. $(0,\emptyset)$ would mean "already held" and would block the very first task; $(n,\emptyset)$ is not binary; $(-1,\emptyset)$ is not even a valid semaphore value.

**Q4. B.** Condition variables have **no stored value** — they are just queues. A `signal` with no waiter is **lost**. A describes a *semaphore* `signal` (which would increment the counter); C and D are nonsense for the event model.

**Q5. B.** Two disjoint fork pairs exist, so $\lfloor 5/2 \rfloor = 2$ philosophers can eat at once. **D is the trap**: `up_to_4` limits *seated* philosophers to 4, but only 2 can hold disjoint fork pairs simultaneously. A is too small; C is impossible with 5 forks.

**Q6. C.** The monitor's single-active-process rule automatically enforces mutual exclusion of its procedures. It does **not** by itself guarantee starvation freedom (A) or deadlock freedom (B) — those depend on the wait/signal protocol used — and it can still lose wake-ups if the code misuses condition variables (D).

**Q7. B.** Mutual exclusion (safety) holds, but liveness fails for writers: if readers keep arriving so `no_of_readers` never returns to 0, `signal(access)` never runs, `access` stays locked, and waiting writers never get in. A and C are false; D is the deadlock (safety) failure mode, which does not occur here.

**Q8. B.** Throughout the no-starvation solution the waker does **not** release `s`; instead it wakes the next process, which "inherits" the lock and later does `signal(s)`. This baton passing both preserves mutual exclusion on the counters and lets one wake-up **cascade** to unblock all parked readers. A and C are false; D is not the reason (the woken process does not re-block on `s.q`).

**Q9.** A **safety** property = "nothing bad happens"; a **liveness** property = "something good eventually happens". **Safety violation:** the naive Dining Philosophers solution **deadlocks** (all five hold their left fork and wait forever) — mutual progress is permanently blocked. **Liveness violation:** the reader-priority Readers–Writers solution **starves writers** — a writer may wait forever while readers flow through. (Either pairing is acceptable if the example genuinely matches the property class.)

**Q10.** If `wait(s)` is implemented as separate "read `s.w`" then "write `s.w−1`" steps, two tasks on a binary semaphore `s=(1,∅)` can both read `s.w = 1`, both decide "free", both decrement, and both enter their critical sections — mutual exclusion is violated. Atomicity makes the check-and-decrement one indivisible operation, so only one task can observe `s.w = 1` and win. (Symmetrically, non-atomic `signal` can corrupt the queue/counter.)

**Q11.** Invariant: `nonempty.w + nonfull.w = n` at all times (items in buffer + free slots = capacity). The **unbounded** buffer can never be full, so the producer never waits — only the consumer can block on an empty buffer, so `nonempty` alone suffices. With a finite buffer, the producer must also be blocked when all $n$ slots are occupied, so `nonfull` (init $n$) is added to count free slots and block the producer when full.

**Q12.** A cyclic index reuses freed slots: after writing slot $n-1$, `in` wraps to $0$. With linear indices, (i) `in`/`out` grow without bound and eventually index **outside the array** (buffer overflow), and (ii) once the producer reaches the end, slots freed by the consumer can never be reused — the buffer reports "full" forever even when empty. `mod n` recycles the slots so a fixed array behaves as a ring buffer.

**Q13.** The two statements describe the same guarantee at different levels. The direct test blocks a reader when a writer is *inside* (`nw > 0`). Writer-starvation prevention comes from the **hand-off**: when the last reader exits (`nr = 0`) and a writer is waiting (`nww > 0`), that reader passes the `s` lock to the writer *without releasing it*. A newly arriving reader then blocks on `wait(s)` before it can even evaluate `nw`, so a **pending writer is guaranteed to run next**. Hence "new readers wait behind a waiting writer" holds — via the lock hand-off rather than via a test on `nww` in the reader's own code.

**Q14.** Because a woken process can only become active *after* the signaller leaves the monitor, and in the meantime the signaller might change the state again. If `signal` is last, the condition the woken process relies on is guaranteed still true at hand-off; if the signaller keeps working after `signal`, the condition may no longer hold when the waiter finally runs.

**Q15.** Using `nonempty.w + nonfull.w = 3` throughout:

| Step | Operation | counter | nonempty.w | nonfull.w | in/out |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | init | 0 | 0 | 3 | in=0, out=0 |
| 1 | P puts `x` | 1 | 1 | 2 | in=1 |
| 2 | P puts `y` | 2 | 2 | 1 | in=2 |
| 3 | C gets (`x`) | 1 | 1 | 2 | out=1 |
| 4 | P puts `z` | 2 | 2 | 1 | in=(2+1)mod3=0 |
| 5 | C gets (`y`) | 1 | 1 | 2 | out=2 |
| 6 | C gets (`z`) | 0 | 0 | 3 | out=(2+1)mod3=0 |

End state: `counter=0`, `nonempty=0`, `nonfull=3`, `in=out=0` → buffer **empty**, and the invariant holds ($0+3=3$). Note step 4 wraps `in` to 0 (slot $n-1$ reused).

*4th put before any consumer:* the producer executes `wait(nonfull)`. With `nonfull.w = 0` (buffer full after 3 inserts), `wait` **blocks** the producer and enqueues it on `nonfull.q`; it stays blocked until a consumer's `signal(nonfull)` increments/awakens it. This is the whole point of the `nonfull` semaphore.

**Q16.** **Deadlock schedule:** all five philosophers execute `wait(fork(i))` (left) successfully before any executes its second `wait`. Each philosopher $i$ then holds fork $i$ and executes `wait(fork((i+1) mod 5))` (right), which blocks because that fork is held by neighbour $i+1$. **Wait-for cycle:** $P_0 \to P_1 \to P_2 \to P_3 \to P_4 \to P_0$. No fork is ever released (no `signal` reached), so all five block permanently. **Why `up_to_4` fixes it:** such a cycle requires **all five** philosophers to be seated mid-meal (the cycle must cover all five forks), so capping the table at 4 seated philosophers makes the cycle impossible — at least one seated philosopher can obtain both forks and eat.

**Q17.** **Possible outputs: `ACB` and `CBA`.** Reason: `B` can only proceed after `signal(s2)`, which only **C** performs, so **`B` always prints after `C`**. Initially `s1 = 1`, so `A` and `C` compete for `s1`:
- **A first:** A takes `s1` (1→0), prints `A`, `signal(s1)` (0→1). Then C takes `s1`, prints `C`, `signal(s2)` → wakes B; B prints `B`, `signal(s1)`. → **`ACB`**.
- **C first:** C takes `s1` (1→0), prints `C`, `signal(s2)` → wakes B. B prints `B`, `signal(s1)` (0→1) → wakes A; A prints `A`. → **`CBA`**.
`ABC`, `BAC`, `BCA`, `CAB` are all impossible because B must follow C.

**Q18.** The fork is at B; the join is at E.

```text
S_B    : semaphore := (0, ∅);   -- A done → start B
S_C    : semaphore := (0, ∅);   -- B done → start C
S_D    : semaphore := (0, ∅);   -- B done → start D
done_C : semaphore := (0, ∅);   -- C done → E
done_D : semaphore := (0, ∅);   -- D done → E

task body A is        task body B is          task body C is
  Operations A;         wait(S_B);              wait(S_C);
  signal(S_B);          Operations B;           Operations C;
end A;                  signal(S_C);            signal(done_C);
                        signal(S_D);          end C;
                      end B;

task body D is        task body E is
  wait(S_D);            wait(done_C);
  Operations D;         wait(done_D);
  signal(done_D);       Operations E;
end D;                end E;
```
A's `signal(S_B)` releases B; B's `signal(S_C)`/`signal(S_D)` release **both** C and D, which then run concurrently (fork); E blocks on **both** `done_C` and `done_D`, so it proceeds only after both finish (join/barrier). (D's order of the two `wait`s is free since it holds no other resource.)

**Q19.** Suppose readers continuously issue requests such that at least one reader is always inside the database. Then `no_of_readers` never returns to 0. `access` is released **only** by a reader executing `signal(access)` when `no_of_readers = 0`, and that condition never occurs. Therefore `access` stays held (value 0) indefinitely, so any writer's `wait(access)` never returns — the writer waits forever even though it could proceed the instant all readers paused. Because a reader never checks whether a writer is *waiting* (it only ever blocks on the first-reader path when `no_of_readers` transitions 0→1), arriving readers keep jumping ahead of waiting writers. Hence a writer can be **starved**. $\blacksquare$

**Q20.** The mutual-exclusion lock would be held by the blocked producer, so **no consumer can enter `get`** to remove an item and execute `signal(nonfull)`. The producer waits on `nonfull`, but the only process that could make the condition true (the consumer) is locked out of the monitor → **permanent deadlock**. `wait` on a condition variable must **release the monitor lock** precisely so that another process can enter and change the state that satisfies the condition.

# Lecture 01 — Proof Cheat-Sheet

Every proof from Lecture 1 as a fill-in template. Read the left column ("what you must
prove"), copy the middle column ("what you write"), and use the right column only when
stuck.

---

## 0. The universal opener

| Situation | First sentence you write |
|---|---|
| proving a $\forall$ statement | "Let $a,b,c\in G$ be arbitrary." |
| proving an implication | "Suppose $X$. We must show $Y$." |
| proving uniqueness | "Suppose $x$ and $x'$ both satisfy the defining property." |
| disproving a $\forall$ | "Take $a=\dots$; then …" (one witness is enough) |
| proving a set is a group | "We verify (G1)–(G3) in order." |

---

## 1. "$(G,*)$ is a group" — six-step ritual

Write the six headings. Do not merge them.

| # | Heading | What must appear |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Well defined** | only if elements are classes: assume $[a]=[a']$, $[b]=[b']$, show $[a*b]=[a'*b']$ |
| 2 | **Closed** | take general $a,b\in G$, show $a*b\in G$ (and *why*: e.g. $a,c\neq0\Rightarrow ac\neq0$) |
| 3 | **Associative** | $(a*b)*c = \dots = a*(b*c)$, naming which associativity of $\mathbb{R}$/$\mathbb{Z}$ you borrow |
| 4 | **Identity** | solve $a*c=a$ for $c$ → candidate $e$; then verify $e\in G$ and $a*e=e*a=a$ |
| 5 | **Inverse** | solve $a*c=e$ for $c$ → candidate; verify $c\in G$; verify $a*c=c*a=e$ |
| 6 | **Commutative** | only if "abelian" is claimed: $a*b=\dots=b*a$ |

Closing sentence: "Therefore $(G,*)$ is a[n abelian] group. $\blacksquare$"

**Never** write a step as "obvious". Each identity/inverse step must *show the algebra
that produced the candidate* — that is the mark.

---

## 2. "This is not a group" — one line per failure

| Failing axiom | Template | Witness to reuse |
|---|---|---|
| closure | "$x=\dots,\ y=\dots\in S$ but $x*y=\dots\notin S$" | $\mathbb{N}$: $3-5=-2$ |
| associative | "$(a*b)*c=\dots\neq\dots=a*(b*c)$" | $\mathbb{Z}$: $(1-2)-3=-4\neq2$ |
| identity | "the only candidate is $e=\dots\notin G$" | $(2\mathbb{Z},\cdot)$: $e=1\notin2\mathbb{Z}$ |
| inverse | "suppose $a*b=e$; then $\dots$, contradiction" | $\mathbb{Q}$: $0\cdot b=0\neq1$; $M_2$: $\det=0$ |
| commutative | "$AB=\begin{bmatrix}8&1\\9&0\end{bmatrix}\neq\begin{bmatrix}2&7\\3&6\end{bmatrix}=BA$" | $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$ |

Also state the positive part: "…although it is closed, associative and has identity $I_2$,
so it is a monoid."

---

## 3. Uniqueness of identity

> Let $e$ and $e_1$ be identities. Since $e$ is an identity, $e_1*e=e_1$. Since $e_1$ is an
> identity, $e_1*e=e$. Hence $e_1=e$. $\blacksquare$

## 4. Uniqueness of inverse

> Let $b,c$ both satisfy $a*b=e=b*a$ and $a*c=e=c*a$. Then
> $$b=b*e=b*(a*c)=(b*a)*c=e*c=c.$$
> Hence $b=c$. $\blacksquare$

**Annotate the four equalities:** identity → substitution $e=a*c$ → associativity →
$b*a=e$ → identity.

## 5. $(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$

**Method A (lecture).** From $a^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=e$, multiply on the left by $a$:
$a\,a^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=a\cdot e$, regroup as $(aa^{-1})(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$, so
$e(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$.

**Method B (faster).** $a$ is an inverse of $a^{-1}$; $(a^{-1})^{-1}$ is also an inverse of
$a^{-1}$; by uniqueness they are equal.

## 6. $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$

**Method A (manipulate).** $(ab)(ab)^{-1}=e$; left-multiply by $a^{-1}$, regroup
$a^{-1}(ab)=b$, left-multiply by $b^{-1}$, get $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$.

**Method B (universal, use this one).** Show both products equal $e$:
$$
(ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1})=a(bb^{-1})a^{-1}=aa^{-1}=e,\qquad
(b^{-1}a^{-1})(ab)=b^{-1}(a^{-1}a)b=b^{-1}b=e .
$$
Then cite **uniqueness of inverses**. $\blacksquare$

*(Method B also proves $c^{-1}=a^{-1}b^{-1}$ style claims instantly: to show
"$X^{-1}=Y$", prove $XY=e=YX$.)*

## 7. Cancellation

> Suppose $ac=bc$. Multiply on the right by $c^{-1}$:
> $(ac)c^{-1}=(bc)c^{-1}\Rightarrow a(cc^{-1})=b(cc^{-1})\Rightarrow ae=be\Rightarrow a=b.$

Mirror for $ca=cb$ with $c^{-1}$ on the **left**. $\blacksquare$

**Trap:** cancellation needs an inverse. In $(\mathbb{Z}_6,\cdot)$,
$2\cdot3\equiv2\cdot0$ but $3\not\equiv0$.

---

## 8. Equivalence relation — three blocks

| Property | Template | Key line |
|---|---|---|
| reflexive | let $a\in A$ | $\frac{a-a}{n}=0\in\mathbb{Z}$ |
| symmetric | suppose $a\equiv b$, say $\frac{a-b}{n}=t\in\mathbb{Z}$ | $\frac{b-a}{n}=-t\in\mathbb{Z}$ |
| transitive | suppose $a\equiv b$, $b\equiv c$, say $\frac{a-b}{n}=r,\ \frac{b-c}{n}=s$ | $\frac{a-c}{n}=r+s\in\mathbb{Z}$ |

Finish: "By (1), (2), (3), $R$ is an equivalence relation. $\blacksquare$"

## 9. Well-definedness of $[a]+[b]=[a+b]$ (the skipped step)

> Let $[a]=[a']$ and $[b]=[b']$. Then $a-a'=nt$, $b-b'=ns$ with $t,s\in\mathbb{Z}$, so
> $a=a'+nt$, $b=b'+ns$. Hence
> $$[a]+[b]=[a+b]=[a'+b'+n(t+s)]=[a'+b']=[a']+[b'],$$
> because $(a'+b'+n(t+s))-(a'+b')=n(t+s)$ is a multiple of $n$.

**Say out loud:** "different representatives give the same class." That is the entire
content.

## 10. $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has exactly $n$ classes

> Every $a$: division algorithm $a=nq+r$, $0\le r<n$ ⇒ $[a]=[r]$.
> No repeats: if $0\le r<s<n$ then $0<s-r<n$ ⇒ $n\nmid(s-r)$ ⇒ $[r]\neq[s]$. $\blacksquare$

## 11. $(\mathbb{Z}_5,+)$ is an abelian group

1. well defined (template §9 with $n=5$)
2. closed: $[a]+[b]=[a+b]$ is a class
3. associative: $[a]+([b]+[c])=[a+(b+c)]=[(a+b)+c]=([a]+[b])+[c]$ — borrowed from $\mathbb{Z}$
4. identity $[0]$: $[a]+[0]=[a+0]=[a]$
5. inverse $[-a]$: $[a]+[-a]=[a-a]=[0]$
6. commutative: $[a+b]=[b+a]$

**Associativity is never readable from a Cayley table** — only closure, identity,
inverses and commutativity are.

---

## 12. Reading a Cayley table (exam one-liners)

- closed ⇔ every cell is an element of $G$
- $e$ ⇔ the row (and column) that copies the header
- $a^{-1}$ ⇔ column where row $a$ meets $e$
- abelian ⇔ symmetric about the main diagonal
- associative ⇔ **cannot** be read off; prove it

---

## 13. Seven traps that cost marks

1. Saying "$\mathbb{Z}$ is a group" without the operation.
2. Proving associativity before closure.
3. Guessing the identity instead of solving $a*c=a$.
4. Verifying $a*e=a$ only on one side when the group is non-abelian.
5. Writing $(ab)^{-1}=a^{-1}b^{-1}$.
6. Calling well-definedness "closure" (or vice versa) for $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
7. Concluding "$X^{-1}=Y$" from $XY=e$ alone without citing uniqueness.

---

## 14. Additive ↔ multiplicative dictionary

| multiplicative | additive |
|---|---|
| $ab$, $a^{-1}$, $e$, $a^n$ | $a+b$, $-a$, $0$, $na$ |
| $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$ | $-(a+b)=(-b)+(-a)$ |
| $(a^{-1})^{-1}=a$ | $-(-a)=a$ |
| $ac=bc\Rightarrow a=b$ | $a+c=b+c\Rightarrow a=b$ |
| $o(a)$: least $n$ with $a^n=e$ | least $n$ with $na=0$ |

- This lecture is the **mathematical toolbox** for the whole course: sets and ordered
  n-tuples, functions (incl. injective/surjective/bijective), predicates, quantifiers,
  and mathematical induction — no automata or machines yet.
- A **predicate** is just a Boolean-valued function ($P: S \to \{0,1\}$ with
  $\text{TRUE}=1$, $\text{FALSE}=0$), and it corresponds *exactly* to a subset
  $R = \{a \in S \mid P(a)\}$ — this predicate↔subset dictionary is used constantly later.
- $\forall x\,P(x)$ is a **conjunction** over the domain (true only if *every* instance
  is true; one counterexample kills it); $\exists x\,P(x)$ is a **disjunction**
  (false only if *every* instance is false).
- Negating a quantifier flips it: $\lnot\forall x\,P(x) \Leftrightarrow \exists x\,\lnot P(x)$
  and $\lnot\exists x\,P(x) \Leftrightarrow \forall x\,\lnot P(x)$.
- **Mathematical induction** = prove $P(1)$ (basis) + prove $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$
  (inductive step); the assumption "$P(k)$ is true" is called the *induction assumption*.
- Sets are **unordered and duplicate-free**; tuples are **ordered** — hence
  $\{1,4,5\} = \{1,5,4\}$ but $(1,4,5) \neq (1,5,4)$, and generally $A \times B \neq B \times A$.

**Intuition first.** A set is a *bag of distinct objects where order doesn't matter*.

  - $x \notin A$ — "$x$ is not an element of $A$"

$$

## TL;DR

- A **sequential program** is a single instruction stream executed by one processor; a **parallel program** decomposes a problem into concurrent tasks across multiple processors.

## Full Detailed Explanation

### 1. Sequential Program (SP)

**Intuition.** A sequential program is the simplest computation model: one instruction stream, one processor, data goes in, results come out.

**Formal definition.** A sequential program $S$ is a finite sequence of instructions that transforms input data satisfying a precondition $p$ into output data satisfying a postcondition $q$. Correctness is expressed as a Hoare triple:

$$\{p\}\; S\; \{q\}$$

where $p$ is the precondition (state of memory before execution) and $q$ is the postcondition (desired state after execution).

**Correctness has two levels:**

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Partial correctness** | For every *terminating* execution of $S$ with input satisfying $p$, the output satisfies $q$. |
| **Total correctness** | Partially correct *and* every execution with input satisfying $p$ terminates. |

Partial correctness does not consider termination — a program that loops forever but never produces wrong output is partially correct.

**Worked examples:**

- $\{x > 0\}\; x := x * 2\; \{x \text{ is even}\}$ — **correct**. If $x > 0$ initially, doubling it always produces an even number.
- $\{x = 5\}\; x := x + 4\; \{x = 10\}$ — **incorrect**. $5 + 4 = 9 \neq 10$.
- $\{k = 5\}\; k := k + 1\; \{k = 6\}$ — **correct**. $5 + 1 = 6$.

### 2. Why Parallel Computing?

Two motivations:

1. **Speedup** — solve complex problems faster by splitting work across processors.
2. **Scale** — solve problems too large for a single machine by partitioning them into pieces that run concurrently.

The entire course revolves around quantifying motivation (1) via speedup, efficiency, and Amdahl's law, and realizing motivation (2) via distributed algorithms.

### 3. Sequential Process

A single task is performed as a **sequential process**: an ordered sequence of operations $o_1, o_2, o_3, \dots$

Key properties:
- The next operation begins only after the previous one completes (no overlap within a single process).
- A sequential process results from executing a single instruction sequence.

This is important because a parallel program is composed of multiple sequential processes — each one is internally sequential, but they run *simultaneously* with respect to each other.

### 4. Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Execution

| Model | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Synchronous** | The caller waits for each operation to finish before proceeding. This forces a sequential order of execution. |
| **Asynchronous** | Operations are not synchronised in time — executions can interleave or overlap. No waiting between processes. |

**Concurrent processes** are sequential processes performed simultaneously and asynchronously: each process is sequential internally, but operations of different processes can occur in any relative order.

This distinction matters because asynchrony introduces the race conditions and critical-section problems that the rest of the lecture addresses.

### 5. Communication Between Processes

#### Shared Memory

All processors share a single global address space. Any processor can read/write any memory location.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P1[Processor 1] --- MEM[Shared Memory]
    P2[Processor 2] --- MEM
    P3[Processor 3] --- MEM
```

*Caption: In a shared-memory system, all processors access the same memory space.*

**Advantages:** fast communication (just a memory read/write), natural for threads on the same machine.

**Challenges:** synchronisation is the programmer's responsibility — this is exactly the critical-section problem.

#### Distributed Memory (Message Passing)

Each processor has its own private local memory. Memory addresses in one processor do not map to another. Processors communicate by sending and receiving messages over a network.

